w: 1 Her clinical cases: health, mucositis or peri-implantitis from the findings Final focus · 6 questions in the bank Know this The one difference between mucositis and peri-implantitis is bone loss beyond the initial remodeling. Both have inflammation, bleeding/suppuration and deeper probing. Dr. Kaur on her part of the comprehensive final (Nov 19), passed on Nov 11; her words, paraphrased. Know the three 2017 definitions cold and be able to tell them apart from a case: inflammation (bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing), probing depth against that implant's baseline (no 3 mm cutoff), and bone against the baseline film (about 2 mm of first-year remodeling is physiologic; loss beyond it with inflammation is peri-implantitis). Practice on the S7 Patient Box cases in the Question Bank (#19, #5, #14, #30 and #31) and S7's High Likelihood list. Peri-implant mucositis, the implant's version of gingivitis. Signs of inflammation; profuse (line or drop) bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; an increase in probing depth compared with baseline; and no bone loss beyond initial remodeling. The deeper pocket comes from inflamed, swollen tissue, not from bone loss. Like gingivitis it is reversible, so take it seriously: don't just put it on watch. A probing depth can only grow for three reasons: an inaccurate measurement, inflammation adding volume to the tissue, or true bone loss. Peri-implantitis. Signs of inflammation; bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; increased probing depth compared with previous exams; and bone loss beyond the crestal changes from initial remodeling. "When somebody talks about peri-implantitis, you should have a picture of true bone loss in your mind." The definition on the slide: a plaque-associated pathological condition in the tissues around implants, characterized by inflammation in the peri-implant mucosa and subsequent progressive loss of supporting bone. The definition itself says the disease runs from inflammation to bone loss, which is why it must be controlled at the mucositis stage. 2 Mucositis vs peri-implantitis: bone loss beyond remodeling is the difference Hint + final focus · 8 questions in the bank Explained under 1 above: Her clinical cases: health, mucositis or peri-implantitis from the findings 3 Health: no 3 mm cutoff; ~2 mm of first-year remodeling is physiologic; compare with the baseline Hint + final focus · 7 questions in the bank Know this There is no 3 mm cutoff for implants: health = no increase in probing depth vs previous exams. Capture the clinical and radiographic baseline. Physiologic vs pathologic bone loss: ~2 mm of crestal remodeling, plateauing in the first year, is normal (the slides give no number; she did). Beyond it = pathologic = peri-implantitis. Peri-implant health. No clinical signs of inflammation (no change in color, no edema, no redness); no bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; no increase in probing depth compared with previous examinations; and no bone loss beyond the crestal bone level changes from initial remodeling. Notice there is no 3 mm cutoff. A healthy implant can probe deeper than 3 mm: the tissue height around it depends on how deep the implant was placed, the height of the abutment, and the tissue itself (a narrow implant in a wide ridge leaves extra tissue). Probing an implant is also hard to do accurately, even with a plastic probe. So every measurement is compared with that implant's own baseline: capture the clinical and radiographic baseline, or you will have nothing to compare to going forward. Crestal remodeling. Once an implant is put in function, the crestal bone adapts to the new load. In class she put a number on it, which the slide doesn't: about 2 mm of remodeling, which plateaus within about the first year. That is physiologic. Any bone loss beyond it is pathologic. 4 Treat it now: suppuration is active disease, mucositis is reversible; why peri-implantitis is hard to treat Hint + final focus · 6 questions in the bank Know this Pus = active disease, at a tooth or an implant: debride (and maybe a local antibiotic). Never 'watch' it. Mucositis is reversible, so treat it too. Suppuration (pus) is a sign of active disease, around a tooth or an implant, and it always needs a response now, whatever the long-term plan: local debridement, and sometimes a local antibiotic at a deep site (Dr. Litz covers antibiotics in Session 8). Why is it so hard to treat? Rebuilding bone around an implant should be easier than true periodontal regeneration: there is no PDL or cementum to regrow, only bone fill, so only osteoblasts are needed. The problem is the surface. Implants are made rough (acid-etched, blasted), even nano-rough, because osteoblasts love it, and so does plaque. No product is better than another at decontaminating the implant surface: saline, chlorhexidine (Peridex), citric acid, EDTA and lasers give the same or similar results. Bone loss around implants also tends not to form the deep, narrow, vertical defects that regenerate best, and disease recurs often. Still, a case with a deep buccal pocket (8-9 mm), suppuration, bleeding and bone loss, but with the mesial and distal bone peaks and the lingual plate intact, is still worth treating: open it, clean it, place a biologic and/or bone graft, cover it with a barrier membrane and close. 5 Bleeding on probing, and radiographs: confirmatory, and the schedule Hint + final focus · 9 questions in the bank Know this Radiographs are confirmatory, not exploratory: baseline at the final restoration, every 6 months in year 1, then annually, plus when PD, BOP or suppuration change. BOP: absence predicts stability; presence shows inflammation but not necessarily progression (force, angulation). Bleeding at 4 of 4 visits: 30%; 0 of 4: 1.5%. Bleeding on probing depends on the tissue's condition and on the probing force. It can be caused by an inappropriate probing force or angulation, or by inflammation of the marginal tissue. Its absence is a good predictor of stable peri-implant conditions; its presence indicates inflammation but may not predict progression. Look at the type of bleeding: a little blood that appears slowly may not mean disease, but profuse bleeding that fills the sulcus as you probe does. Track it over visits. In the study on the slide, sites that bled at 4 of 4 visits had a 30% chance of attachment loss; 3 of 4, 14%; 2 of 4, 6%; 1 of 4, 3%; and sites with no bleeding at any of 4 visits, 1.5%. Bleeding on probing is a limited but useful prognostic indicator. Radiographs are taken at: implant placement; before the Phase II uncovery surgery (or before the prosthetic phase if one-stage); the final impression; final abutment seating; the final cementation or restoration (the baseline radiograph); every 6 months for the first year; and annually after that. Extra radiographs are indicated at a maintenance visit when the clinical signs point to disease: increased probing depth, bleeding on probing, suppuration. "Radiographs are confirmatory rather than exploratory" (Lang and Hill 1977): read them together with the clinical findings. 6 Smoking and implants: pathogens, immunity, nicotine, the studies A professor's hint · 8 questions in the bank Smoking works on three fronts. Microbiology: smokers harbor different, more virulent plaque bacteria, and A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis and B. forsythus are harder to eradicate in current smokers; smoking depletes oxygen, and the gram-negative anaerobes love that. Immunology: impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, fewer T helper cells and B lymphocytes, more IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and more collagenase activity. Physiology: nicotine impairs revascularization in soft and hard tissue, the first step of healing after surgery. The numbers: Bain and Moy 1993, 2,194 implants, failure rate 11.3% in smokers vs 4.76% in nonsmokers; Alsaadi 2007, a dose-response relationship, with worse rates in heavy smokers; Simonis 2010, peri-implantitis in 23.53% of smokers vs 16.51% of nonsmokers. Dose-response means the higher the dose, the worse the outcome: years of smoking and cigarettes a day both count, and risk starts below a pack (20) a day. Vaping: little long-term evidence; there is no combustion, so the vasoconstrictive effect on healing may be missing, but the immune response is still suppressed. 7 Risk assessment at every stage; treat periodontitis before implants A professor's hint · 7 questions in the bank Know this A patient who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host carrying the same pathogens. Untreated periodontitis = contraindication; treated, arrested, compliant = implants are fine (her conclusion). Her own end-of-class list of what to know: smoking; mucositis vs peri-implantitis; bone loss as the key difference; physiologic vs pathologic bone loss; and risk assessment at every stage (before placement, during osseointegration, in maintenance, after removal). Yes, it matters. A patient who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host, and susceptibility to periodontal disease raises the risk of peri-implant disease, even in a fully edentulous mouth. Putative periodontal pathogens may persist even a year after periodontally involved teeth are extracted. Definitive treatment of periodontitis is critical to success, and untreated periodontitis is a contraindication to implant therapy. A patient whose periodontitis has been treated and is in maintenance can receive implants like anyone else, with a maintenance plan matched to their risk. Risk assessment is done before implant placement, during the osseointegration period, during implant maintenance, and after the removal of an implant: at every stage, not once. Any risk factor that increases the risk of periodontitis also increases the risk of implant failure, and untreated or partially treated periodontal disease leads more often to implant failure. 8 Success vs survival; Albrektsson's criteria Core of the lecture · 5 questions in the bank Know this Survival = the implant is present and restored (loaded) and can still have biologic or prosthetic complications. Success = no complications at all. Know Albrektsson's criteria: immobile, no radiolucency, no pain/infection/paresthesia/neuropathy, ≤1.5 mm bone loss at 1 year (then <0.2 mm a year). "Be cautious of the terms used, success versus survival." A surviving implant is simply present in the mouth and restored, in other words loaded. A surviving implant can still have biologic complications (peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, bone loss, inflammation) and prosthetic complications (a fractured abutment, a loose screw, a fractured crown, even a fractured implant), or simply pain or mucosal recession. A successful implant is restored and free of any complication, clinically and radiographically. When you read implant studies, check which one they measured. The success criteria on the slide are Albrektsson's, from 1986: the implant is immobile; there is no peri-implant radiolucency; there is no pain, infection, paresthesia or neuropathy; and after 1 year in function, vertical bone loss is 1.5 mm or less. In class she added the rest of the criterion: after that first year, no more than 0.2 mm of vertical bone loss a year. A radiolucency at the apical third of an implant is called retrograde peri-implantitis. 9 Ailing, failing, failed; a mobile implant comes out Core of the slides · 8 questions in the bank Know this Mobile implant = failed = remove it. First confirm the mobility is in the implant body, not the abutment or crown. Peri-implantitis itself rarely makes an implant mobile. This classification describes the implant's state and tells you what to do. An ailing implant has static radiographic bone loss with no inflammation and no mobility: the loss stopped, on its own or because someone intervened. Monitor it, and capture the clinical and radiographic data at each visit. A failing implant has progressive bone loss and signs of inflammation, but no mobility: it is still in function, and what you do varies case by case (for example, keep an 89-year-old's implants at #18 and #19 when taking them out would leave too little bone above the inferior alveolar nerve to rebuild). A failed implant has progressive bone loss, clinical mobility and loss of function. Unlike a tooth, a mobile implant has only one treatment: remove it. Mobility of the implant body means loss of osseointegration, which "nobody in this universe can reverse." First confirm the mobility is in the implant body, not the abutment or the crown. Loss of osseointegration is usually not from peri-implantitis: implants rarely become mobile from peri-implantitis, even with only a third of the implant left in bone. An implant with bone loss that advanced is still judged failed, mobile or not, when it has no future. 10 Plaque biofilm, microbiology and the risk factor lists Core of the slides · 8 questions in the bank Know this Peri-implant disease is multifactorial, but plaque biofilm is the primary cause; periodontitis and peri-implantitis share pathogens. Peri-implant disease is multifactorial, but "if somebody has to ask you" how it starts, the answer is bacteria: plaque biofilm. Periodontitis and peri-implantitis share causative bacteria. The slide groups the risk factors as patient-related, surgical/implant-related, soft tissue and prosthetic. Risk factors for peri-implant mucositis (slide): smoking (current or former), history of periodontitis, active periodontitis, thin soft tissue phenotype, and obesity and/or metabolic syndrome. Risk factors for peri-implantitis: smoking (current or former), history of periodontitis, active periodontitis, obesity and/or metabolic syndrome, implant malposition, uncontrolled diabetes, limited bone width, and depression or antidepressant medications. Poor plaque control carried an odds ratio of 14.3 (Ferreira et al. 2006). Other factors on the slide: systemic disease, lack of keratinized tissue and parafunctional habits. 11 Diabetes: control (HbA1c), not duration Core of the lecture · 4 questions in the bank Know this Smoking: dose-response. Diabetes: control (HbA1c, 3-4 months = red cell lifespan) matters, duration doesn't; poorly controlled = contraindicated. Diabetes. The duration of diabetes did not affect implant survival under optimal glycemic control. A periodontally healthy environment is essential along with good glycemic levels, and implant therapy is contraindicated with poorly controlled diabetes. The measure is glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), the gold standard, because it reflects the last 3-4 months, the lifespan of red blood cells. Get the lab value for your records. (Not part of the lecture, she added: UAB's clinic uses an HbA1c of 8 or higher as a contraindication, and a patient's value can come down, so keep reassessing.) 12 IL-1 genotype, and with smoking Review guide · 2 questions in the bank From the class exam-review guide (not in this year's slides): IL-1 gene polymorphisms are linked to a hyper-responsive inflammatory reaction to bacteria, and a positive IL-1 genotype plus smoking has a synergistic effect, the highest peri-implantitis risk. In class she listed genetic traits and a family history of periodontitis among the risk factors to weigh. You can skip UAB's clinic cutoff (HbA1c ≥8) was an aside, not lecture content. The lecture's point: poorly controlled diabetes contraindicates implants, measured by HbA1c.
